growth.why_this_wins: A current 2026 NASA research hook adds freshness to an evergreen, universally understandable infrastructure-risk premise. The story has a clean beauty-to-danger contrast, strong myth-busting value, multiple escalating systems, and rich diagrammatic visual potential without requiring sensational apocalypse claims.
growth.core_paradox: The most beautiful visible effect of the storm can be the least important part; the real danger is invisible current and degraded infrastructure underneath it.
growth.hook_promise: Start with beautiful worldwide auroras, then escalate through satellites, navigation, radio, power-grid stress, and the surprising parts modern infrastructure can actually survive.
critic_lessons_applied: Open on a concrete visual event before explanation.
Escalate through distinct systems rather than repeating the same consequence.
Use the phone-does-not-explode myth break as a mid-video curiosity reset.
End by snapping back to the beautiful-sky opening image.
fact_risks: Do not describe the event as a universal EMP.
Do not promise a worldwide blackout or years-long recovery.
Keep the 2026 Nature/NASA result framed as challenging an assumed ceiling, not proving unlimited effects.
growth.topic: What if the strongest solar storm we can realistically get hit Earth?
